lesson.title: 1. It lives up to the hype
lesson.context: ***Context:*** *Emily has been telling her friend Jake to watch Parasite for months. He finally watched it last night, and now they’re having coffee.*
lines: So, did you finally watch it?
I did. You were right. It definitely **lives up to the hype**.
What did you think of the first half?

At first, I thought it was just **a dark comedy** about a poor family tricking a rich one. Then **halfway through**, there’s that huge **plot twist**, and the whole film changes. I **didn’t see it coming** at all.
That’s why I didn’t tell you anything. I didn’t want to **spoil it for you**.
I’m glad. I didn’t even watch **the trailer**. The director’s really clever. He **keeps you on the edge of your seat**, but you’re still laughing.
And **the cast** is brilliant. Everyone **gives a great performance**. I think there isn’t really **a villain**. Everyone’s just trying to survive.

I also loved **the cinematography**. The rich family’s house is so bright and clean, and the poor family’s flat is half underground. Even **the camera angles** show you who’s at the top and who’s at the bottom.
Did you notice all the stairs? The poor family is always walking down.

I didn’t notice that. I might have to watch it again. **Funnily enough**, I nearly didn’t watch it at all, because I usually hate **subtitles**. But I’d rather read subtitles than watch it **dubbed**.
Same. And it was **the first non-English film to win Best Picture** at the Oscars, so it must be worth the effort.
It **deserved** it. The only thing is **the ending**. It’s not exactly **a feel-good film**. So what should I watch next?
His earlier film, *Memories of Murder*. But I’m not telling you anything about it.
vocab: It definitely **lives up to the hype**.

lesson.title: 2. A book that stays with you
lesson.context: ***Context:*** *Hà’s English colleague, Tom, sees an old Vietnamese novel on her desk at lunchtime.*
lines: Is that a Vietnamese novel? I’ve never seen you reading at lunch before.
Only sometimes. It’s *Tắt đèn*, by Ngô Tất Tố. We had to read it at school, but I wanted to **read it again as an adult**.
What’s it **about**? The cover looks a bit **gloomy.**

It is. It’s **set in** a village in northern Vietnam in the 1930s, **under French colonial rule**. **The main character**, Chị Dậu, is a poor farmer’s wife. Her husband is **seriously ill**, and they **can’t afford** to pay the yearly tax, so the village officials **drag him away** and beat him.
That’s awful. So what does she do?
She tries everything to **raise the money**. In the end, she **has no choice but to** sell her seven-year-old daughter to a rich family.
Wow, that’s really dark. I had to read Oliver Twist at school, and I thought that was depressing.

This is probably worse. I still remember the scene when the officials come back for her husband. At first, she begs them politely, but when they **push her too far**, she **fights back** and knocks them to the ground.
Good for her. They're **driving her into a corner.**
Yeah. We even have a saying for it: *tức nước vỡ bờ*. It means that if you push people too hard, they’ll **eventually** fight back.
So does it have **a happy ending**, or **is that asking too much**?

I won’t **give** too much **away**, but no, not really. It’s quite **bleak**. Still, it **paints a vivid picture of** how hard life was for ordinary people back then. It’s **stayed with me** since I was fourteen.
Is there an English translation? I might **give it a go**.
I think so. I’ll look it up for you.

homework.title: Part 1: Vocab check
homework.instructions: Fill in each blank with a phrase from the word bank. Use each phrase once.
homework.context: Vy has just watched the film version of her favourite novel. She’s telling her friend Nam about it over coffee.
lines: So, how was the film? You’ve been waiting ages to see it.
Honestly, it really {lived up to the hype}. I was worried they’d ruin the book, but they didn’t.
What’s it about? I’ve never read it.
It {is set in} a small village in central Vietnam in the 1980s. It’s about two brothers growing up in a poor family.
It’s quite slow-paced, but the {cinematography} is stunning. Every scene looks like a painting: green rice fields, yellow flowers everywhere.
The boy who plays the older brother {gave a great performance}. He was only twelve, but he made the whole cinema cry.
Is it exactly the same as the book?
Mostly. But the director added one scene that isn’t in the book, and I {didn’t see it coming} at all.
I’m not telling you. I don’t want to {spoil it for you}.
Fair enough. Is it a happy film?
It’s not exactly a {feel-good film}, but it isn’t completely {bleak} either. It {paints a vivid picture of} childhood in the countryside: the games, the jealousy, the first crush.
It is. I watched it a week ago, and it’s really {stayed with me}. Watch it first, and then read the book.

homework.title: Part 2: Listening
homework.intro: Listen to a short film review, then do Parts A and B.

script.text: Welcome back to Weekend Watch. This week, I finally watched Coco, the Pixar film that came out in 2017. I know, I'm very late. My niece has been asking me to watch it with her for years, and ==I kept saying it looked like a film for little kids.==

I was wrong. Coco is about Miguel, a twelve-year-old boy in Mexico who dreams of ==becoming a musician==. The problem is that his family has ==banned music== for generations, because ==his great-great-grandfather left the family to follow his music career==. On the Day of the Dead, Miguel accidentally ends up in the Land of the Dead, where he meets his ancestors and a funny, slightly dishonest man called Héctor.

To be honest, the first twenty minutes didn't grab me. ==The story felt quite familiar==: a kid who wants to follow his dream while his family says no. But once Miguel crosses into ==the Land of the Dead==, the film really comes alive. The animation is stunning. The whole city glows with orange and purple lights, and ==I kept pausing the film just to look at the backgrounds.==

Then, about an hour in, there's a ==plot twist== that completely changes how you see two of the main characters. I won't spoil it, but my niece, who's seen it ten times, was watching my face the whole time.

What really got me, though, was the ending. There's a scene where a song called "==Remember Me==" is sung to a very old woman, and I'm not ashamed to say I had to reach for the tissues. ==My niece, meanwhile, was eating popcorn as if nothing was happening.==

My only complaint is that ==the villain becomes a little too obviously evil== once you know the truth. But that's a small thing. It's a beautiful film about family, memory and never forgetting the people we love. ==Nine== out of ten from me.

questions.q: Why hadn’t the speaker watched Coco before?
options: Her niece didn’t want to watch it with her.
She thought it was aimed at young children.
She doesn’t usually enjoy films about music.
questions.why: “I kept saying it looked like a film for little kids.”

questions.q: Why is music banned in Miguel’s family?
options: A man in the family chose music over his wife and children.
Héctor persuaded the family that music was dangerous.
Music isn’t allowed during the Day of the Dead.
questions.why: “His great-great-grandfather left the family to follow his music career.”

questions.q: What did the speaker think of the first part of the film?
options: The animation was the best part.
It moved too quickly for her niece.

questions.q: What did the speaker do because of the animation?
options: She watched some scenes again with her niece.
She stopped the film to enjoy the scenery.
She looked at her niece’s face to see her reaction.
questions.why: “I kept pausing the film just to look at the backgrounds.”

questions.q: How did the niece react to the ending?
options: She cried as much as the speaker did.
She watched the speaker’s face closely.
She didn’t seem emotional at all.
questions.why: “My niece, meanwhile, was eating popcorn as if nothing was happening.”

questions.q: What is the speaker’s criticism of the film?
options: The plot twist is too easy to guess.
One character becomes too clearly bad.
The film is too long for young children.
questions.why: “The villain becomes a little too obviously evil once you know the truth.”
